sections.overview: The common swift is a bird built around open air: it catches food, drinks, gathers nest material and often rests while flying. Its brief breeding season is the exception, when a pair returns to a cavity to raise its young. The species usually raises one brood in a year, then leaves its European breeding grounds for Africa as summer ends.
sections.identification: In British adults, the mean wing length is about 175 mm and mean body mass is 39.5 g. Their sooty-brown plumage, pale throat, long swept-back wings and short forked tail form a dark, curved silhouette overhead; the small throat patch is easily missed as they speed past.
sections.habitat: It breeds across much of Europe and Asia, nesting in enclosed spaces such as roof gaps, eaves, old walls, cliffs and tree hollows. In Britain and Ireland, swifts nest almost entirely in buildings, where roof cavities can support colonies even in busy towns. Outside the breeding season, tracked birds range across sub-Saharan Africa, with winter destinations differing among European populations.
sections.diet: The swift takes flying insects and spiders, from aphids and flies to beetles and small wasps, sweeping them from the air with its wide gape. Adults accumulate many tiny prey in a saliva-bound throat pouch, then regurgitate the compact food bolus to their chicks; its contents change with the insects available. Both adults forage in the air and bring this concentrated meal back to the nest, where several small prey items arrive together rather than one at a time.
sections.behavior: Long, narrow, sickle-shaped wings and short feathered feet suit rapid, agile flight and gliding, while making take-off from level ground difficult. Swifts call with piercing screams as they wheel in social groups near nest sites. Tracking showed that during the ten-month non-breeding period, tagged birds spent over 99% of their time airborne; this does not describe the breeding season. Most tracked birds nevertheless showed occasional periods without flight.
sections.reproduction: A pair lays a usual clutch of two or three eggs in a shallow cup of feathers and plant fibres glued with saliva inside a cavity. Both parents incubate for about 18–24 days and feed the naked, helpless hatchlings. Young normally leave the nest after roughly 37–56 days, with timing affected by conditions; they then fly independently. The species generally rears a single brood during its short stay on the breeding grounds.
sections.ecology: By feeding on airborne arthropods, swifts are tied to weather: cold or prolonged rain can make prey harder to find and adults less able to forage, leaving nestlings short of food. Researchers have confirmed occasional nocturnal torpor in families resting in nests during cold breeding-season nights; torpor is a temporary, controlled reduction in metabolism, not a routine state for every bird. In a monitored Italian colony, nestling survival also varied with hatching order and brood conditions, showing how a spell of poor feeding can affect the youngest chicks.
sections.conservation: BTO monitoring shows that British breeding numbers fell by 70% between 1995 and 2024. Building renovations close roof gaps and remove nest sites; this loss contributed to the swift’s addition to the UK red list in 2021.
